s1.syndrome_frame: Acute abdominal pain with peritonism and sepsis
salient_findings: Multi-organ involvement with lymphadenopathy and pulmonary consolidation
key_facts: 60-year-old man with history of heavy cigarette smoking
History of emphysema, hypertension, and prostate cancer in remission
Presented with 4-hour history of acute right lower-quadrant abdominal pain
Fever of 38.5°C on admission
Hypotensive with systolic blood pressure 90 mmHg
Tachycardic with heart rate 110/min
Peritonism in the right lower quadrant on examination
Perforated appendix with collection and surrounding fat stranding on CT
Innumerable hepatic nodules and lymphadenopathy on CT
Pulmonary consolidation and collapse in the right lower lobe on CT
Underwent exploratory laparotomy with subtotal colectomy and end ileostomy
Remained ventilated postoperatively
Failed extubation attempt on day 3

shortlist.why_kept: Perforated appendix with peritonism and sepsis

shortlist.label: Perforated viscus
shortlist.why_kept: Perforated appendix with peritonism and sepsis

shortlist.why_kept: Peritonism and sepsis with perforated viscus

shortlist.label: Sepsis

shortlist.label: Colorectal cancer
shortlist.why_kept: Thickened, woody sigmoid colon and lymphadenopathy on CT

raw.rationale: The patient presented with fever, hypotension, and tachycardia, which are classic signs of sepsis, and had a perforated appendix with peritonitis, leading to a systemic inflammatory response

rejected.label: Acute appendicitis
rejected.why: While the patient had a perforated appendix, this is a contributing factor to the sepsis rather than the primary diagnosis

rejected.label: Perforated viscus
rejected.why: This is a more general term that encompasses the perforated appendix, but does not fully capture the systemic response

rejected.label: Peritonitis
rejected.why: The patient had peritonitis, but this is a localized infection and does not fully explain the systemic signs of sepsis

rejected.label: Colorectal cancer
rejected.why: While the patient had a thickened sigmoid colon, the primary issue was the perforated appendix and resulting sepsis, rather than the cancer
